sections.h2: What happens to a reverse mortgage when the borrower dies?
sections.html:
The loan balance becomes due and payable. HUD's heirs flyer says the loan must be satisfied by the thirtieth day after the borrower dies, and the lender may approve 90-day extensions if the estate or heirs show they are actively trying to sell or repay (HUD, Inheriting a Home Secured by an FHA-insured HECM).

A HECM, or Home Equity Conversion Mortgage, is the reverse mortgage insured by the Federal Housing Administration. While the borrower lives in the house no payments are due, and the balance comes due when the borrower sells, stops using the home as their main home, or dies as the last surviving borrower. HUD adds that no more funds may be paid out once that point is reached.

Those 30 days run out long before most Florida probate cases finish. Call the loan servicer first, ahead of any court filing.

sections.h2: How does a HECM work while the borrower is alive?
sections.html:
HUD describes the HECM as the only reverse mortgage insured by the federal government, available through an FHA-approved lender (HUD HECM page). Borrowers may live in the home indefinitely as long as property taxes and homeowner's insurance stay current.

The amount a borrower can draw depends on three inputs:

  • the age of the youngest borrower or eligible non-borrowing spouse;
  • the current interest rate;
  • the lesser of the appraised value, the FHA mortgage limit or the sales price.

Heirs who are weighing a sale should ask whether the borrower fell behind on taxes or insurance, since that is a common reason servicers call a loan due. HUD points people toward free counseling at (800) 569-4287 and warns against paying scam artists for information that HUD provides at no charge.

sections.h2: What choices do Florida heirs have?
sections.html:
Heirs, other than a non-borrowing spouse, can pay off the loan, sell the home, or hand the property to the lender by a deed in lieu to head off foreclosure. The estate carries property taxes and insurance until title moves.

OptionWhat HUD's flyer says
Sell the homeIf the balance exceeds the home's value, a sale at 95 percent or more of current appraised value lets the lender accept the net proceeds as full payment
Keep the homeThe loan balance must be paid off in full
Deed in lieuTitle goes to the lender to avoid foreclosure
Extension90-day extensions possible with proof of active efforts to sell or repay

Source: HUD flyer dated September 2019. The flyer says any post-death transfer is treated as a "sale" for the 95 percent rule.

sections.h2: What if the borrower's spouse is still living in the house?
sections.html:
A non-borrowing spouse may have extra protection. HUD says special provisions can postpone repayment, allowing the spouse to remain in the property during their lifetime, but the spouse must give the lender a Non-Borrowing Spouse Certification in the first 30 days after the last surviving borrower dies, among other requirements.

That 30-day clock is the one most easily missed during a funeral week. If you are a surviving spouse who was not on the loan, contact the lender and the FHA Resource Center at (800) 225-5342 (listed on the HUD flyer) before any other paperwork.

Whether a particular spouse qualifies depends on conditions that the lender can explain, so ask for them in writing.

sections.h2: What should heirs line up before calling a buyer?
sections.html:
Having the facts in hand lets a buyer, the servicer and the title company work from the same numbers. Gather the following before any offer is accepted:

  • a certified copy of the death certificate and the loan number;
  • the servicer's current payoff figure, which should be requested in writing;
  • proof that taxes and insurance are current, since HUD's flyer leaves those costs with the estate;
  • a current appraisal, because the 95 percent figure is measured against appraised value;
  • the personal representative's name and, where probate is open, a copy of the letters from the court.

If the lender has granted a 90-day extension, keep the paperwork showing active efforts, such as the listing agreement or a signed purchase contract. HUD's flyer ties any extension to that kind of proof, so the file should be ready for the servicer on request.

Heirs who disagree about selling should resolve that early. A servicer's clock keeps running while relatives argue, and only a person with legal authority over the estate can sign a deed.

sections.h2: How does Florida probate affect selling the house?
sections.html:
The house usually sits in the decedent's name, so someone needs legal authority to sign. Florida offers summary administration when the non-exempt estate does not exceed $150,000 or the decedent has been dead more than 2 years (s. 735.201), and formal administration otherwise. Your county probate clerk can say which route fits the house.

Two Florida facts shape the timing:

  • A creditor loses the right to claim unless it files by the later of two dates: 3 months after the notice to creditors is first published, or 30 days after a creditor entitled to direct notice is served (s. 733.702). The reverse mortgage lender is a secured lender, so ask the servicer how it will proceed.
  • Deeds signed by a personal representative under a probated will are on the state's not-taxable list for documentary stamps (DOR page).

Florida has no estate tax for people who died after December 31, 2004, and since July 1, 2023 personal representatives need not file Form DR-312 or DR-313 (DOR estate tax page).

sections.h2: What if the lender starts foreclosure?
sections.html:
Florida foreclosures go through the courts. After a final judgment the clerk sells the property at public sale not less than 20 days or more than 35 days after judgment unless the plaintiff agrees to a longer period, and the high bidder posts a 5 percent deposit (s. 45.031).

Heirs who want to avoid that path have the hand-the-keys option noted above. Keep every letter from the servicer and answer court papers on time, because a missed deadline limits what you can still do.

A sale before judgment usually leaves the most room. A buyer who closes quickly can pay off the HECM balance at closing, and a buyer taking the house in current condition suits an estate that cannot fund repairs.

sections.h2: Does a reverse mortgage change the property tax picture?
sections.html:
The borrower's homestead benefits depend on the home staying the permanent residence. Homestead is lost, the state says, if the home is rented, stops being the permanent home, or the owner is no longer a Florida permanent resident (DOR homestead guidance).

Once the borrower has died, a sale or transfer of title is a change of ownership, so assessed value resets to just value the next January 1 unless an exception applies. HUD's flyer reminds heirs that taxes and insurance stay with the estate until title transfers, so budget for them.

To plan your numbers, ask the lender for a payoff statement, ask a licensed appraiser for a current value, and ask the county property appraiser how assessments will change.

faqs.q: How long do heirs have to pay off a HECM?
faqs.a: HUD's heirs flyer says the loan must be satisfied within 30 days of the borrower's death, and the lender may approve 90-day extensions with documentation of active efforts to sell or repay.

faqs.q: Do heirs owe more than the house is worth?
faqs.a: HUD's flyer says that if the balance exceeds the home's value, heirs may sell for at least 95 percent of the current appraised value and the lender will accept the net proceeds as satisfaction of the loan.
Yes, if the HECM balance is paid off in full. HUD says that is the condition for keeping the home.

faqs.q: What can a surviving spouse who was not on the loan do?
faqs.a: HUD says special provisions may allow the spouse to stay for life, but a Non-Borrowing Spouse Certification is due to the lender in the first 30 days after the last borrower's death.

faqs.q: Who pays property taxes on the house after the borrower dies?
faqs.a: HUD's flyer states that property taxes and insurance remain the responsibility of the borrower's estate until title is transferred.
